title: Color & White Balance

learn.summary: Light has color temperature, measured in kelvin: candlelight glows around 1900 K, tungsten bulbs 3200 K, daylight about 5500 K, open shade 7000 K and up. White balance is the camera compensating so whites stay white — or your deliberate refusal to compensate, for mood. Color decisions are exposure decisions' quieter twin.

do: Photograph one white object under three light sources today (sunlight, household bulb, phone flashlight) with auto white balance off or locked, and compare the casts.

children.title: White Balance Control

learn.summary: Auto white balance guesses — and it guesses wrong at sunsets (neutralizing the gold you came for) and under mixed lighting. Presets (daylight, cloudy, tungsten) or a manual kelvin dial give you the vote back. Shooting RAW makes white balance losslessly re-decidable in the edit; JPEG bakes it in.

do: Shoot one sunset or lamp-lit scene twice this week — auto white balance versus a locked "daylight/sunny" setting — and see which kept the warmth.

children.title: Color Harmony

learn.summary: Complementary pairs sitting opposite on the color wheel — orange/teal, red/green, yellow/purple — create instant visual tension, which is why cinema grades lean orange-and-teal. Analogous schemes (neighboring hues) soothe instead. A photo with two strong colors nearly always beats a photo with six weak ones.

do: Hunt one complementary color pair in the wild this week (orange jacket against blue wall, red leaf on green grass) and build a photo around it.

children.title: Shooting for Mood

learn.summary: Warm casts read as nostalgia, intimacy, and evening; cool casts read as distance, melancholy, and dawn — and you can choose the lie: setting white balance to "cloudy" warms a scene, "tungsten" plunges daylight into cinematic blue. Accurate color is a default, not a law. Decide the emotion first, then pick the temperature that serves it.

do: Take one scene and produce a warm version and a cool version (white-balance presets or editing sliders), then title each with the emotion it now carries.

children.title: Monochrome Seeing

learn.summary: Strip color away and photographs run on tone, shape, texture, and contrast alone — which is why black-and-white is a perennial teaching tool, not nostalgia. Scenes with strong graphic bones (shadows, silhouettes, geometry) gain power in mono; scenes whose whole point was color simply die. Many phones offer a live mono filter so you can see tonally while shooting.

do: Shoot for 30 minutes this week with your camera set to a live black-and-white filter — not converted after — and keep your three strongest frames.
